summary: A pointer is a variable whose value is the memory address of another object, and the dereference operator follows that address to read or write the object. Pointers let functions modify the caller's data, let you allocate memory at run time, and make linked lists, trees, graphs, callbacks and generic code possible. They are also the main source of crashes in C: uninitialized, null, dangling and out-of-range pointers all lead to undefined behavior. Operating systems, drivers, embedded firmware and language runtimes are built on them.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.body:
Every variable lives at some address in memory. A pointer is a variable that stores such an address instead of an ordinary value. With the address operator `&` you get the address of an object, and with the dereference operator `*` you reach the object at an address. That small pair of operators is what makes C a systems language: you can name memory directly, hand a function the location of your data instead of a copy, build structures out of nodes that refer to each other, and treat code itself as an address you can call.

A pointer carries two pieces of information: the address, and the type it points to. The type tells the compiler how many bytes to read on dereference and how far to step in arithmetic. The address itself is just a number of the machine's word size, so every pointer on a 64-bit system takes 8 bytes whatever it points to.

sections.heading: Core Concepts
bullets: **Address**: the numeric location of a byte in the process's virtual address space. Printed with `%p`, cast to `void *`.
**Pointer variable**: `int *p;` declares `p` as able to hold the address of an `int`. The `*` here is part of the declaration.
**Address-of `&`**: `&x` produces the address of object `x`, of type `int *` when `x` is an `int`.
**Dereference `*`**: `*p` is the object `p` points to. It can be read (`y = *p`) or written (`*p = 5`).
**Pointer type**: determines the size of the access on dereference and the scale factor in arithmetic. `int *` reads 4 bytes, `char *` reads 1.
**Pointer size**: 4 bytes on a 32-bit system and 8 bytes on a 64-bit system, independent of the pointed-to type.
**Null pointer**: a pointer that points to no object, written `NULL` or `0`. Dereferencing it is undefined behavior.
**Void pointer**: `void *` can hold the address of any object type but cannot be dereferenced or used in arithmetic (without a GNU extension) until converted back to a concrete type.
**Wild pointer**: declared but never initialized, so it holds garbage.
**Dangling pointer**: still holds the address of an object whose lifetime has ended, such as freed heap memory or a returned local variable.
**Pointer to pointer**: `int **pp` holds the address of an `int *`, and `**pp` reaches the int.
**Pointer to const versus const pointer**: `const int *p` cannot change the target through `p`, while `int *const p` cannot be re-pointed.

sections.heading: How It Works
sections.body:
Take `int var = 10; int *ptr = &var;` on a 64-bit machine. Suppose `var` is at address 0x7ffc1000. The compiler stores 10 in those 4 bytes, and stores the number 0x7ffc1000 in the 8 bytes of `ptr` (which sit at some other address, say 0x7ffc1008). `*ptr` means: read `ptr`, treat its value as an address, load an `int` from there, giving 10. `*ptr = 20;` stores 20 at 0x7ffc1000, so `var` becomes 20 even though `var` was never named. Two names for one object is called aliasing.

The classic use is output parameters. C passes arguments by value, so a function receiving `int a` can only change its own copy. If it receives `int *a`, it receives a copy of the address and can change the original through it. The swap function below shows both the mechanism and the call syntax.

sections.heading: Variants & Types
bullets: **Typed data pointers**: `int *`, `char *`, `double *`, `struct node *`. The type gives the stride for arithmetic and the width for access.

**`void *`**: the generic pointer returned by `malloc` and accepted by `memcpy` and `qsort` comparators. In C it converts implicitly to and from any object pointer, so no cast is needed. C++ requires a cast.
**Null pointer**: the 'points nowhere' value, used for list ends, optional arguments and error returns.
**Wild and dangling pointers**: not special types but states you must avoid.
**Pointer to pointer**: needed when a function must change which object a caller's pointer refers to, or for arrays of strings such as `char **argv`.
**Pointer to const / const pointer / const pointer to const**: `const int *p`, `int *const p`, `const int *const p`. Read declarations right to left.
**Function pointer**: `int (*fp)(int, int) = add;` holds the address of code. Called with `fp(1, 2)`. Basis of callbacks, dispatch tables and `qsort`.
**Pointer to array**: `int (*pa)[5] = &a;` points to a whole 5-int array, so `pa + 1` skips 20 bytes.
**Pointer to struct**: use `p->field`, which is shorthand for `(*p).field`.
**Integer-pointer conversions**: `uintptr_t` from `<stdint.h>` can hold a pointer's value. Casting back is implementation-defined.

sections.heading: Complexity & Costs
bullets: **Dereference**: one memory load or store, O(1), but its real cost depends on cache. An L1 hit is about 4 cycles, main memory about 100 ns or 200+ cycles.
**Pointer size**: 8 bytes on 64-bit, so a linked list of 4-byte ints spends 8 bytes on the link (plus padding), tripling the memory of an array.
**Pointer chasing**: following `next` pointers defeats prefetching, so a list traversal is often 10 to 100 times slower per element than an array scan.
**Passing by pointer**: copying 8 bytes of address instead of a large struct, so 1 KB structs cost the same to pass as an int.
**Aliasing**: when the compiler cannot prove two pointers refer to different objects it must reload values after each store. `restrict` tells it they do not, enabling vectorization.
**Indirection levels**: each `*` in `int ***p` is another dependent load, so three-level lookups cost three serial memory accesses.
**Pointer comparison and copy**: O(1) and a single register operation.

sections.heading: Common Pitfalls & Gotchas
bullets: **Uninitialized (wild) pointer**: `int *p; *p = 5;` writes to a random address. Initialize every pointer, to a valid address or `NULL`.
**Dereferencing NULL**: undefined behavior, in practice a segmentation fault on most systems. Check `malloc` and API results before use.
**Dangling pointer after `free`**: `free(p); *p = 1;` is use-after-free. Set `p = NULL` after freeing.
**Returning the address of a local**: `int *f(void) { int x = 1; return &x; }` returns a pointer to a dead stack slot.
**Wrong format**: printing a pointer with `%d` is undefined. Use `%p` and cast to `void *`.
**The declaration trap**: `int* a, b;` makes `a` a pointer but `b` a plain int. Write `int *a, *b;`.
**Confusing `*` roles**: in a declaration `*` makes a pointer type, in an expression it dereferences, and between two operands it multiplies.
**Memory leak by overwriting**: `p = malloc(10); p = malloc(20);` loses the first block.
**Type punning through casts**: reading an `int` object through a `float *` violates strict aliasing and can be miscompiled. Use `memcpy` or a union.
**Mismatched pointer types**: `int *p = (int *)&some_char_array;` can trigger misaligned access faults on strict architectures.
**Comparing or subtracting unrelated pointers**: only defined within one array or object.

sections.heading: Real-World Use
bullets: **Dynamic data structures**: linked lists, trees, graphs and hash chains are nodes joined by pointers.
**Output parameters and large arguments**: `scanf("%d", &n)`, `fread(buf, 1, n, f)`, `pthread_create(&tid, ...)`.
**Callbacks**: `qsort`, signal handlers, event loops and driver tables hold function pointers.
**Hardware access**: memory-mapped registers are accessed through `volatile uint32_t *` pointers fixed to device addresses.
**Zero-copy data paths**: network stacks pass packet buffers by pointer and move header pointers instead of copying bytes. The Linux `sk_buff` is such a structure.
**Opaque handles**: libraries return `FILE *` or `struct foo *` without revealing the layout, which is encapsulation in C.
**Kernel object graphs**: `container_of` converts a pointer to an embedded `list_head` back to its enclosing struct.

sections.heading: Interview Notes
bullets: **Q: What is a pointer?** A variable that stores the address of another object, with a type saying how to interpret what lives there.
**Q: Size of a pointer?** 4 bytes on 32-bit, 8 on 64-bit, the same for every object pointer type on common platforms.
**Q: Difference between `*p++`, `(*p)++` and `*++p`?** `*p++` reads then advances the pointer, `(*p)++` increments the pointee, `*++p` advances then reads.
**Q: Wild versus dangling versus null?** Wild was never initialized, dangling points to released storage, null points to nothing on purpose.
**Q: Why `void *`?** Generic containers and allocators. It must be converted back to a concrete pointer before dereferencing.
**Q: Pass-by-value or pass-by-reference in C?** Always by value. Passing a pointer simulates reference semantics by copying the address.
**Q: What is `int *const p` versus `const int *p`?** The first freezes the pointer, the second freezes the data seen through it.
**Q: How to modify a caller's pointer?** Pass a pointer to it, `int **pp`, and assign `*pp`.

sections.body: Declare with `type *name;`, initialize with `name = &object;` or `= NULL`, and use `*name` for the pointee. The `*` in the declaration and the `*` in an expression are different roles of one symbol. The type of `&x` is pointer to the type of `x`, and dereferencing and taking the address cancel out: `*&x` is `x`.
sections.code:
int var = 10;
int *p = &var;      // declaration with initializer
*p = *p + 5;        // var is now 15
int *q = p;         // q and p alias var
*q += 1;            // var is 16
int *n = NULL;      // safe, points nowhere

subtopics.title: Pointer sizes and printing
subtopics.summary: Why every pointer is the same size and how to print one correctly.

sections.body: The size equals the machine's address width: 8 bytes in an LP64 or LLP64 64-bit build. A pointer to `char`, `double` or a giant struct are all 8 bytes, because each stores only an address. Print with `%p` and cast to `void *`, because `%p` expects exactly that type. Addresses differ from run to run on modern systems because of address space layout randomization (ASLR).

subtopics.title: Null, void, wild and dangling pointers
subtopics.summary: The four special states every C programmer has to tell apart.

bullets: **Null**: `int *p = NULL;` guaranteed unequal to any valid object address. Test with `if (p)` or `if (p == NULL)`.
**Void**: `void *v = &x;` stores any address. Convert with `*(int *)v` to read.
**Wild**: `int *p;` holds garbage. Any dereference is undefined behavior.
**Dangling**: after `free(p)` or when a function returns, the pointer still holds the old address. Reset to `NULL` when you release the object.
Each of these four is common in interview 'spot the bug' questions.

subtopics.title: Pointers and function arguments
subtopics.summary: Pass by value, simulated reference, and the double-pointer case.

sections.body: A function parameter is a copy. To let a function change the caller's int, pass its address. To let it change which node the caller's pointer refers to, for example inserting at the head of a list, pass the address of the pointer. Forgetting this is the classic bug where an allocation inside the function never reaches the caller.

subtopics.title: Pointers and arrays
subtopics.summary: Why an array name behaves like a pointer, and where it does not.

sections.body: An array name decays to the address of element 0, so `int *p = a;` works and `p[i]` equals `a[i]`. Differences remain: `sizeof a` is the whole array, `sizeof p` is 8, `a` cannot be assigned, `&a` has pointer-to-array type. The arrays and pointer arithmetic lessons go deeper, but remember the equality `a[i] == *(a + i)`.

subtopics.title: Constant pointers and pointers to const
subtopics.summary: Reading const declarations right to left.

sections.body: `const int *p`: p points to an int that cannot be changed through p, but p may move. `int *const p`: p is fixed to one address, the pointee may change. `const int *const p`: neither. `int *const p = &a; p = &b;` fails with an error about assigning to a read-only variable. Use `const` on pointer parameters of functions that only read, such as `size_t strlen(const char *s)`, to document and enforce intent.
sections.code:
int a = 1, b = 2;
const int *pc = &a;   // *pc = 5 is an error; pc = &b is fine
int *const cp = &a;   // *cp = 5 is fine;    cp = &b is an error
const int *const cc = &a;   // both are errors

subtopics.title: Multilevel pointers
subtopics.summary: Double and triple pointers, with an example you can trace.

sections.body: `int **pp = &p;` stores the address of `p`. `*pp` is `p`, `**pp` is the int. The common real uses are `char **argv`, a function that returns a pointer through an output parameter, and a dynamically allocated 2D array built as an array of row pointers. Each extra level adds one load and one more way to leak or dangle.

A function name decays to its address, like an array name. Declare `int (*op)(int, int);`, assign `op = add;` (or `&add`) and call `op(10, 5)`. The parentheses around `*op` matter: `int *op(int, int)` declares a function returning `int *`. Dispatch tables, `qsort(base, n, size, cmp)` and callbacks use this. See the Function Pointers lesson for more.

subtopics.title: Pointers to structs
subtopics.summary: Arrow syntax and building linked structures.

sections.body: For `struct node *n`, write `n->next` instead of `(*n).next`. A struct containing a pointer to its own type is what makes lists and trees. Initialize `next` to `NULL` so traversal knows where to stop. Free nodes one at a time, saving `next` before freeing the current node.

subtopics.title: Debugging pointer bugs
subtopics.summary: Tools and habits that find wild, null and dangling accesses.

bullets: Compile with `-Wall -Wextra -g` and read warnings about uninitialized use and incompatible pointer types.
Run with AddressSanitizer: `-fsanitize=address,undefined` reports use-after-free, out-of-bounds and null dereference with a stack trace.
Run under Valgrind (`valgrind --leak-check=full ./a.out`) for uninitialized reads and leaks.
In gdb, `p *ptr`, `p ptr`, `x/8xb ptr` and `bt` after a crash show what the pointer held.
Set pointers to `NULL` after `free`, and assert non-null preconditions at function entry.

takeaways: A pointer stores an address; `&x` gets one, `*p` follows one, and `*&x` is just `x`.
All object pointers on a 64-bit platform are 8 bytes, whatever they point to; the type controls access width and arithmetic stride.
C passes by value, so a function modifies caller data only through a pointer, and modifies a caller's pointer only through a pointer to it.
Wild (never initialized), dangling (object gone) and null pointers all give undefined behavior on dereference; initialize to NULL and reset to NULL after free.
`const int *p` protects the data, `int *const p` protects the pointer; read declarations right to left.
`int* a, b;` declares one pointer and one int; put the `*` next to each name.
Never return the address of a local variable, and never print a pointer with `%d`; use `%p` with a `(void *)` cast.
Use `->` for struct pointers and a double pointer when a function must update the caller's pointer.
